why: The neither/nor proximity concord rule is stateable and decides any sentence of this shape.
Sequence of tenses: the earlier past action takes the past perfect — a rule, not a remembered sentence.
a/an is decided by initial sound, a rule that generalises to any word once you can pronounce it.
Which preposition 'responsible' takes is an arbitrary collocation, not something derivable from the adjective's meaning.
Active-to-passive is a mechanical transformation preserving tense; the rule generalises to any sentence.
Reported speech applies stateable shifts to tense, pronoun and time word.
One-word substitution: nothing about the definition yields 'polyglot' if the word was never learnt.
The figurative sense of 'meridian' is lexical knowledge with no derivation path.
Antonym item — knowing 'frugal' and 'extravagant' is pure vocabulary recall.
English spelling is conventional; no rule distinguishes the correct letter doubling here.
Punctuation of direct speech is settled by stateable rules on comma, capital and mark placement.
Grammar eliminates two options, but the live affect/effect choice is a lexical confusable a competent user can still get wrong.
Idiomatic meaning of 'shelve' is arbitrary; it cannot be worked out from the words.
The too...to / so...that equivalence is a transformation rule that applies to unseen sentences.
Choosing the connector requires reasoning about the logical relation between the two clauses.
Sentence type follows from counting independent versus subordinate clauses — derivable once clause types are understood.
Part of speech follows from what the word does in the sentence, not from a memorised list.
The mandative subjunctive is a stateable rule that generalises, though which verbs trigger it is partly lexical.
Third conditional: past perfect in the if-clause fixes 'would have + participle' in the main clause.
The choice follows from what each modal means — 'must have' is the deductive one.
Prohibition versus absence of obligation is a meaning distinction between modals, reasoned not recalled.
A verb after a preposition takes the gerund — a rule that applies to any verb.
Causative 'make' takes the bare infinitive, a stateable rule, though membership of the bare-infinitive verb set is lexical.
'Each' governs the verb regardless of the intervening of-phrase — a concord rule that generalises.
'Since' plus continuing action forces the present perfect; the rule decides any such sentence.
Superlatives take 'the' by rule; the river-names convention is more of a class list, so labelled medium.
Phrasal-verb meaning is an arbitrary collocation — 'call off' is not deducible from 'call' plus 'off'.
Passive transformation preserving the present perfect is rule-governed and generalises.
Reporting a wh-question applies known shifts plus the statement word-order rule.
One-word substitution: 'teetotaller' must have been learnt; the definition does not generate it.
Synonym item — the meaning of 'pragmatic' is lexical recall.
Antonym item — 'transient' must be known; the distractors are all its synonyms.
principal/principle is a spelling confusable; the noun sense has to have been committed to memory.
Idiom meaning is arbitrary and cannot be reasoned out from the literal words.
Degree transformation is rule-governed: 'higher than any other' maps onto the superlative.
The perfect participle for a completed prior action by the same subject is a rule that generalises.
Classifying by coordinator plus two independent clauses follows from what 'compound' means.
The contraction rule decides it ('it's' = 'it is'), though its/it's is also a heavily confused pair.
Word class follows from the joining function 'and' performs in the sentence.
Spelling is conventional; no rule rules out the plausible-looking misspellings.
